column2: This coin isn't fair. It lands heads four times in five. Alice and Bob have to settle a bet with it, and neither of them knows how unfair it is. There's a way to do it that is perfectly fair, using nothing but this coin.
The obvious way is to call it. Alice says heads, Bob gets tails, one toss decides. In a thousand tosses, heads comes up seven hundred ninety-one times. Alice wins about four bets in five.
Then let Bob call heads. But that only helps if they know which side the coin favours. With a strange coin, they don't.
A real coin, tossed and caught, can't be made this unfair. A coin spun on a table can. So can a loaded die, or the noisy circuit inside a computer. Our coin stands for all of them.
So here's the puzzle. One unfair coin, and nobody knows how unfair. How would you get a fair decision out of it?
Toss the coin twice, and look at the two results as a pair.
A pair can be four things. Two heads. Heads then tails. Tails then heads. Two tails.
Draw their chances as areas. The first toss splits a square from left to right. Heads gets four fifths of the width.
The second toss splits it from bottom to top, at the same mark, because it's the same coin.
Two heads is the big block, sixty-four percent. Two tails is the small one, four percent. What about heads then tails, against tails then heads?
Sixteen percent each. Exactly equal.
So play it like this. Alice calls heads then tails. Bob calls tails then heads. If the pair matches, throw it away and toss two more.
A thousand games with our coin. Alice wins four hundred ninety-four. Bob wins five hundred six.
The coin is as unfair as ever. The game isn't.
Why exactly equal? Heads then tails is four fifths times one fifth. Tails then heads is one fifth times four fifths.
The same two numbers, multiplied in the other order. And multiplying doesn't care about order.
Make the coin worse. Ninety percent heads. Are the two blocks still equal?
Yes. Slide the cut wherever you like. One block is always the mirror image of the other.
In letters, call the chance of heads p. Heads then tails is p times one minus p. Tails then heads is one minus p times p. Equal for every p.
So nobody needs to know how unfair the coin is, or even which side it favours.
The trick does lean on two things. The coin's chance is the same on both tosses, and one toss doesn't affect the next. Tosses like that are called independent.
The trick has a price. Most pairs get thrown away. With our coin, a pair decides only thirty-two times in a hundred.
So how many tosses does a game take, on average?
Six and a quarter. Here are ten thousand games. They average six point two one.
A fair coin would need four tosses. A coin that's ninety-nine percent heads needs about a hundred and one.
And no game is sure to end by any given toss. About one game in fifty is still going after ten pairs. The longest of our ten thousand ran thirty pairs. Sixty tosses.
Could a cleverer rule always stop after ten tosses? No. Picture a coin that almost never lands tails. Ten heads in a row is then almost certain, so whoever wins on ten heads almost always wins.
Now break it. Toss our unfair coin first, and a fair coin second. Is heads then tails still level with tails then heads?
No. One cut moved and the other didn't, so the blocks aren't mirror images any more. Forty percent against ten. Alice wins four games in five, as if they'd never bothered.
A sneakier break is a coin with a memory. Say it repeats its last result four times in five.
After two heads, heads then tails takes one change of face. Tails then heads takes two. So it's four times as likely. Anyone who saw the pair that was thrown away knows who's about to win.
Real coins have a touch of this. A tossed coin comes up the way it started about fifty-one times in a hundred.
The cure is to compare like with like. Pair up only the tosses that come straight after a head, and the trick is fair again.
Go back to why the trick works. Heads then tails and tails then heads are made of the same results, one head and one tail. Only the order is different.
And order never changes a chance. Take three tosses. Two heads then a tail. Heads, tails, heads. A tail then two heads. Which is likeliest?
None of them. Each is point eight, times point eight, times point two, in some order. Same counts, same chance.
So sort every pattern by how many heads it has. For two tosses, the groups hold one, two and one. The middle group is our trick.
For three tosses, one, three, three, one. For four, one, four, six, four, one.
The coin's unfairness decides which group you land in. Our coin usually lands in a group with lots of heads. But inside a group, every pattern is equally likely, for any coin at all.
The counts carry the unfairness. The order is perfectly fair.
Look at the middle of row four. Six patterns, all equally likely. What else has six equally likely outcomes?
A die. Toss the coin four times. If exactly two are heads, the pattern picks the face. If not, toss four more.
Twenty-four thousand tosses of our unfair coin made nine hundred forty-nine rolls of a fair die. Each face came up about one time in six.
It isn't cheap. A coin that loves heads rarely gives exactly two in four. It works about fifteen tries in a hundred, so a roll costs twenty-six tosses on average.
There are cheaper recipes. But the idea is what matters. Any group of patterns with the same counts is a fair choice among them.
Now swap the coin for a loaded die. This one shows a six half the time.
Can Alice and Bob get a fair decision from it?
Roll it twice. If the two rolls match, roll again. If not, Alice wins when the first roll is bigger, and Bob wins when the second is.
It's the coin trick again. Two different results are as likely one way round as the other. A coin is just a die with two faces.
Three rolls do more. If all three are different, they came in one of six orders. Smallest first, biggest first, and so on. Six orders, equally likely. That's a fair die, made from a loaded one.
And it keeps going. Four different rolls can come in twenty-four orders. Five, in a hundred and twenty.
Here's the picture behind that. Three rolls pick a point in a cube, and the die's chances slice it along every side.
A four, a five and a six, in each possible order, land in these six bricks. How do the bricks compare?
They're one brick, turned six ways. A tenth, by a fifth, by a half. Same volume, so the same chance.
One loose end. The two toss trick throws most of the coin away. A hundred tosses of our coin give about sixteen fair ones. How many could the best possible rule get?
Seventy-two. That ceiling is called the coin's entropy, and no rule beats it.
You get closer by wasting less. Use the bigger groups in deeper rows of the triangle. Or pick up the pairs you threw away, and run the trick again on them.
Both climb toward seventy-two, and never quite arrive.
The two toss trick is John von Neumann's. He gave it in a talk in nineteen forty-nine, in a single paragraph.
He named the price too. Suppose the coin was fair all along. How much of it does the trick waste?
Three tosses in four. In his words, at most twenty-five percent as efficient as ordinary coin tossing.
Computers took him at his word. In nineteen ninety-nine, Intel's hardware random number generator ran its raw, lopsided bits through a corrector built on this trick.
So an unfair coin still has a fair one inside it, as long as it can land both ways. You find it by ignoring what came up, and looking only at the order.
